domains.summary: The largest domain on the PTCE (35% as of the January 6, 2026 outline). Focus on brand/generic pairs, drug classifications, mechanisms of action, indications, side effects, interactions, contraindications, insulin types, and storage. Dedicated NTI-list items are no longer a standalone knowledge area.

sections.title: Top Drug Classes & Suffixes
items: ACE inhibitors (-pril): lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril — hypertension, heart failure. Watch for dry cough, hyperkalemia, angioedema.
ARBs (-sartan): losartan, valsartan, olmesartan — alternative to ACE inhibitors; less cough.
Beta blockers (-olol): metoprolol, atenolol, carvedilol — hypertension, angina, heart failure; don't stop abruptly.
Calcium channel blockers: amlodipine (-dipine), diltiazem, verapamil — hypertension; non-DHP cause bradycardia/constipation.
Statins (-vastatin): atorvastatin, simvastatin, rosuvastatin — lower LDL; myopathy, ↑LFTs. Nystatin is an antifungal, not a statin.
Proton pump inhibitors (-prazole): omeprazole, pantoprazole, esomeprazole — GERD, ulcers; take before meals. Aripiprazole is not a PPI.
H2 blockers (-tidine): famotidine — heartburn.
SSRIs: sertraline, fluoxetine, escitalopram, paroxetine — depression, anxiety; serotonin syndrome risk.
Benzodiazepines (-pam/-lam): lorazepam, alprazolam, diazepam, clonazepam — anxiety, seizures (C-IV controlled).
Fluoroquinolones (-floxacin): ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin — tendon rupture black box, avoid dairy/antacids.
Macrolides (-thromycin): azithromycin, clarithromycin — QTc prolongation.
Tetracyclines (-cycline): doxycycline — photosensitivity, avoid dairy.
DPP-4 (-gliptin), SGLT-2 (-gliflozin), GLP-1 (-glutide): diabetes agents.
Triptans (-triptan): sumatriptan — migraine; CI in CAD.
-olol suffix = beta blockers (e.g., metoprolol, propranolol).

sections.title: Mechanisms of Action by Class
items: ACE inhibitors: block angiotensin-converting enzyme → ↓ angiotensin II → vasodilation.
ARBs: block angiotensin II receptor.
Statins: inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → ↓ cholesterol synthesis.
PPIs: irreversibly block H+/K+ ATPase proton pump.
Beta blockers: block beta-adrenergic receptors → ↓ HR, ↓ contractility.
Calcium channel blockers: block L-type Ca channels → vasodilation.
Loop diuretics (furosemide): inhibit Na-K-2Cl in loop of Henle.
Warfarin: inhibits vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X).
Heparin: activates antithrombin III.
Metformin: ↓ hepatic glucose production, ↑ insulin sensitivity.
Sulfonylureas: ↑ pancreatic insulin secretion.
SSRIs: block serotonin reuptake.
Triptans: 5-HT1B/1D agonists → cranial vasoconstriction.
MAOIs: block monoamine oxidase → tyramine crisis + serotonin syndrome risk.
Levodopa/carbidopa: dopamine precursor; carbidopa blocks peripheral breakdown.
Allopurinol: inhibits xanthine oxidase → ↓ uric acid production.

sections.title: Common Brand / Generic Pairs
items: Lipitor = atorvastatin
Prinivil/Zestril = lisinopril
Glucophage = metformin
Synthroid = levothyroxine
Prilosec = omeprazole
Norvasc = amlodipine
Coumadin = warfarin
Lasix = furosemide
Zoloft = sertraline
Neurontin = gabapentin
Ventolin/ProAir = albuterol
Zithromax = azithromycin
Eliquis = apixaban
Xarelto = rivaroxaban
Plavix = clopidogrel
Januvia = sitagliptin
Jardiance = empagliflozin
Ozempic/Wegovy = semaglutide
Cymbalta = duloxetine
Wellbutrin = bupropion
Lyrica = pregabalin
Advair = fluticasone/salmeterol
Augmentin = amoxicillin/clavulanate
Flexeril = cyclobenzaprine
Sinemet = carbidopa/levodopa
Zyloprim = allopurinol
Imitrex = sumatriptan
Lipitor = atorvastatin.

sections.title: Insulin Types
items: Rapid-acting: lispro (Humalog), aspart (NovoLog), glulisine (Apidra) — onset ~15 min; give with meals.
Short-acting: regular (Humulin R, Novolin R) — onset ~30 min; only insulin safe IV.
Intermediate: NPH (Humulin N, Novolin N) — cloudy; peak 4–10 hr; mix last.
Long-acting (basal): glargine (Lantus/Basaglar), degludec (Tresiba) — clear; do NOT mix. Detemir (Levemir) is discontinued in the US.
Concentrated: Toujeo (glargine U-300), U-500 regular — NOT interchangeable unit-for-unit.
Storage: unopened refrigerated 36–46°F; do NOT freeze; opened may be kept at room temp for a limited time per product.
Rapid-acting: lispro, aspart, glulisine — onset ~15 min; mealtime.
Long-acting: glargine — about 24 hours, no pronounced peak. Degludec lasts at least 42 hours.
Unopened insulin: refrigerate. In-use Lantus vial: 28 days, refrigerated or room temperature. In-use Lantus SoloStar: 28 days at room temperature only (do not refrigerate). Never freeze.

sections.title: Common OTC Active Ingredients
items: Tylenol = acetaminophen (max 4,000 mg/day; hepatotoxic in overdose).
Advil/Motrin = ibuprofen (NSAID; take with food).
Aleve = naproxen (NSAID).
Claritin = loratadine; Zyrtec = cetirizine; Allegra = fexofenadine (2nd-gen antihistamines).
Benadryl = diphenhydramine (1st-gen; sedating).
Sudafed = pseudoephedrine (CMEA logbook; ↑ BP; behind counter).
Mucinex = guaifenesin (expectorant); Delsym = dextromethorphan (antitussive).

sections.title: Key Side Effects & Monitoring
items: ACE inhibitors: dry cough, hyperkalemia, angioedema.
Statins: myopathy/rhabdomyolysis, ↑ LFTs.
Metformin: GI upset, lactic acidosis (rare).
Corticosteroids: hyperglycemia, adrenal suppression, osteoporosis, weight gain.
Fluoroquinolones: tendon rupture, QTc, peripheral neuropathy.
Metoclopramide: tardive dyskinesia (black box), EPS.
Pioglitazone: HF exacerbation, bladder cancer risk.
Bisphosphonates: esophageal irritation — stay upright 30 min, empty stomach.
ACE inhibitors (e.g., lisinopril) — dry, persistent cough.

sections.title: Critical Interactions & Contraindications
items: MAOI + SSRI/SNRI/triptan/tramadol/linezolid/dextromethorphan → serotonin syndrome.
MAOI + tyramine foods (aged cheese, wine, cured meats) → hypertensive crisis.
Warfarin: antidote vitamin K; monitor INR; many CYP + dietary (vitamin K) interactions.

Metformin: hold at the time of or before iodinated contrast only if eGFR is 30–60, or there is a history of liver disease, alcoholism, or heart failure, or the contrast is intra-arterial; recheck eGFR at 48 hours and restart if stable (lactic acidosis).
Methotrexate: WEEKLY dosing for RA — daily = fatal error.
Nitroglycerin + PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil) → severe hypotension.
St. John's Wort induces CYP3A4 → ↓ OCPs, warfarin, many drugs.
Triptans/ergots: contraindicated in CAD, uncontrolled HTN.
PPIs (omeprazole) ↓ clopidogrel activation (CYP2C19).
Abacavir: HLA-B*5701 test before use (hypersensitivity).
Grapefruit inhibits CYP3A4, raising levels of statins, calcium channel blockers, and other substrates.

sections.title: Vaccine Storage
items: Varicella: frozen (-50°C to -15°C). MMR: refrigerate 2–8°C; M-M-R II may be refrigerated or frozen. Live vaccines: CI in pregnancy/immunocompromised.
Inactivated influenza, Shingrix, pneumococcal, Tdap, Hep B: refrigerate 2–8°C.
COVID-19 mRNA: frozen/ultra-cold per product.
Rule: most vaccines refrigerate and must not be frozen; varicella must be frozen; M-M-R II may be refrigerated or frozen.

sections.title: Narrow Therapeutic Index (NTI) Drugs
items: OPTIONAL / ARCHIVE — not emphasized on the January 6, 2026 PTCE. Removed as a dedicated PTCE knowledge area on the January 6, 2026 outline (old 1.8). Still useful as high-alert / monitoring context, not as a standalone NTI-list drill.
Classic examples: warfarin, digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, theophylline, levothyroxine, carbamazepine, valproic acid, tacrolimus, cyclosporine, aminoglycosides, vancomycin.
These agents often need therapeutic drug monitoring; treat them as high-alert rather than memorizing a standalone NTI roster.

sections.title: Known Teratogens (Pregnancy Safety)
items: isotretinoin (iPLEDGE), thalidomide, warfarin, methotrexate, valproic acid, phenytoin, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, tetracyclines, lithium, misoprostol. Statins are not an absolute avoid: stop them in most pregnant patients and weigh the individual need.

sections.title: Dosage Forms & Routes
items: Sublingual (SL): dissolves under tongue, rapid absorption, bypasses first-pass (nitroglycerin). Buccal = between cheek and gum.
Enteric-coated: resists stomach acid, dissolves in small intestine — do NOT crush (aspirin EC, omeprazole).
Extended-release (ER/XL/SR/CR/LA): releases over time — do NOT crush or chew (risk of dose dumping). TOPROL-XL is scored and may be split; do not crush or chew it.
Orally disintegrating tablets (ODT) dissolve on the tongue; effervescent tablets must be dissolved in water first.
Transdermal patches: steady absorption, bypass first-pass; rotate sites, do not cut reservoir patches, fold before disposal (fentanyl).
Suppositories (rectal/vaginal) bypass first-pass partially; store some refrigerated. Many metered-dose inhalers need priming; ProAir RespiClick does not.

Suspensions: "shake well before use." Reconstituted antibiotic suspensions are not all refrigerated. Amoxicillin: discard after 14 days; refrigeration is preferable, not required. Azithromycin oral suspension: 5–30°C (41–86°F), use within 10 days.
Sublingual (SL): under the tongue for rapid absorption; nitroglycerin is a classic example.

sections.title: Respiratory, Psych & Miscellaneous Agents
items: SABA rescue: albuterol (ProAir, Ventolin). ICS maintenance: fluticasone (Flovent). LABA: salmeterol (never alone in asthma).
Montelukast (Singulair): leukotriene antagonist for asthma/allergic rhinitis; boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects.

SSRIs (no single class suffix; examples: fluoxetine (Prozac), sertraline (Zoloft)) — take weeks to work; risk serotonin syndrome with MAOIs/triptans. -oxetine is not SSRI-only (duloxetine is an SNRI).
SNRIs: duloxetine (Cymbalta) — depression, anxiety, neuropathic pain; venlafaxine (Effexor XR) — MDD, GAD, social anxiety, and panic, not neuropathic pain.
Benzodiazepines (-azepam/-azolam): alprazolam (Xanax), lorazepam (Ativan) — C-IV, sedation/dependence; reversed by flumazenil.
Z-hypnotics: zolpidem (Ambien), eszopiclone (Lunesta) — C-IV for insomnia.
SGLT2 inhibitors (-gliflozin): empagliflozin (Jardiance) — diabetes; watch genital infections, DKA. GLP-1 agonists: semaglutide (Ozempic).

Thiazolidinediones (-glitazone): pioglitazone (Actos). Biguanide: metformin (Glucophage) — first-line T2DM. Contrast hold is only for higher-risk patients (eGFR 30–60, liver disease, alcoholism, heart failure, or intra-arterial contrast).
Alpha-1 blockers (-azosin/-ulosin): tamsulosin (Flomax) for BPH — first-dose orthostatic hypotension.

sections.title: Musculoskeletal, Bone & Gout
items: NSAIDs: ibuprofen (Advil/Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), meloxicam (Mobic), celecoxib (Celebrex) — GI bleed risk; take with food.
Bisphosphonates: alendronate (Fosamax) for osteoporosis — take with plain water 30+ min before food, stay upright.
Allopurinol (Zyloprim): xanthine oxidase inhibitor for chronic gout prevention. Colchicine for acute gout flares.
Acetaminophen (Tylenol) max 4 g/day (many use 3 g); hepatotoxicity in overdose — antidote N-acetylcysteine.

domains.summary: Patient Safety and Quality Assurance (23.75% as of the January 6, 2026 outline). Covers error prevention, high-alert and LASA drugs, ISMP error-prone abbreviations, hygiene, reporting, and technician-relevant USP/hazardous-drug handling. Dedicated nonsterile compounding procedures are no longer a core knowledge area.

sections.title: High-Alert & LASA Drugs
items: High-alert (ISMP): insulin, anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin, DOACs), opioids, concentrated electrolytes (KCl), chemotherapy, neuromuscular blockers, methotrexate, digoxin.
LASA examples: hydrOXYzine vs hydrALAZINE, predniSONE vs prednisoLONE, DOPamine vs DOBUTamine, vinBLAStine vs vinCRIStine, Celebrex vs Cerebyx — use tall-man lettering.
Independent double-check required for all high-alert meds.
High-alert classes: anticoagulants, insulin, opioids, neuromuscular blockers, chemotherapy.

sections.title: Error Prevention Basics
items: Five rights: right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, right time (+ documentation, reason).
Use 2 identifiers: full name and date of birth.
Barcode scanning verifies the correct product against the order.
Independent double-checks for high-alert meds (e.g., insulin, heparin).
Medication reconciliation compares a patient's meds to new orders to prevent duplication/omission.
Pharmacist performs final verification; a tech cannot verify their own work.

sections.title: ISMP Error-Prone Abbreviations (Avoid)
items: 'U' or 'u' → write 'units' (can look like 0 or 4).
'IU' → write 'international units'.
'QD'/'QOD' → write 'daily'/'every other day'.
Trailing zero (1.0 mg) → write 1 mg.
No leading zero (.5 mg) → write 0.5 mg.
'MS/MSO4/MgSO4' → spell out morphine sulfate or magnesium sulfate.
'μg' → write 'mcg'; 'cc' → write 'mL'; 'D/C' spell out; 'hs' → 'at bedtime'.
'OD/OS/OU' → write 'right eye'/'left eye'/'both eyes'. 'AD/AS/AU' → write 'right ear'/'left ear'/'both ears'.

sections.title: Medication Error Types & DUR
items: Outline 3.5 examples: incorrect dose, quantity, patient, drug, and route. Wrong time and omission are other error types; they are not the outline examples.
Process types: prescribing, transcription/entry, dispensing, administration, monitoring errors; near-miss = caught before patient.
Adverse drug event (ADE): harm from a drug (may or may not be an error).
Prospective DUR: BEFORE dispensing — interactions, allergies, duplication, dose.
Concurrent DUR: during therapy; Retrospective DUR: after dispensing (audits).
OBRA-90 (effective 1993): for each Medicaid beneficiary or caregiver who presents a prescription, prospective DUR and an offer to counsel. Not limited to new prescriptions.

sections.title: USP Chapter IDs (2026 scope)
items: USP <795> (non-sterile compounding chapter): dedicated nonsterile compounding procedures were removed from the January 2026 PTCE outline — do not treat BUD tables or compounding technique as core tested skills.
USP <797> is the sterile compounding chapter. Cleanroom categories, ISO class drills, and garbing are CSPT-level — not core 2026 PTCE. Do not treat Category 1 vs Category 2 as required exam content.
USP <800> hazardous-drug handling has been official since December 1, 2019 (not December 1, 2023): containment, PPE, and spill kits.
Optional garbing enrichment only, dirtiest to cleanest: shoe covers → hair/beard cover → mask → hand hygiene → gown → sterile gloves.

sections.title: Quality Assurance & Reporting
items: Report errors/near-misses to improve systems (non-punitive culture).
MedWatch: FDA adverse event reporting; FAERS public database; ISMP MERP; VAERS for vaccines.
Root Cause Analysis (RCA): investigates WHY (reactive); FMEA: proactive failure analysis.
PPE donning: gown → mask → goggles → gloves; doffing: gloves → goggles → gown → mask.
Tall Man lettering distinguishes LASA pairs (e.g., hydrALAZINE vs hydrOXYzine).

sections.title: Reporting Programs
items: FDA MedWatch: voluntary reporting of adverse events, product problems, medication errors (Form 3500 professionals / 3500B consumers).
ISMP MERP: voluntary, confidential national error reporting to identify and share prevention strategies.
NCC MERP error categories: A potential → B no reach → C reach/no harm → D monitoring to confirm no harm and/or intervention to preclude harm → E–I increasing harm (I = death).
Report near misses (intercepted errors) too — they reveal system weaknesses before harm occurs.

sections.title: Quality Improvement Methods
items: Root cause analysis (RCA): systems-based review to find underlying process failures (not individual blame) after an error.
PDSA cycle (Plan-Do-Study-Act): iterative method to test and refine quality improvements.
Independent double checks: two qualified staff separately verify high-alert meds before dispensing/administration.
Prospective DUR screens before dispensing; retrospective DUR reviews prescribing/dispensing patterns afterward.
Medication reconciliation at every transition of care prevents omissions, duplications, and dose errors.

sections.title: Infection Control & Hazardous Materials
items: Hand hygiene: soap + water for at least 20 seconds; alcohol-based rub when hands not visibly soiled.
Sharps: rigid, puncture-resistant, closable sharps containers; never recap used needles by hand.
NIOSH maintains the list of hazardous drugs (antineoplastics, hormones, some antivirals).
Hazardous-drug PPE: two pairs of chemotherapy-tested gloves + impermeable gown; eye/face/respiratory protection per risk.
Counting trays and countertops (3.6): wipe with 70% isopropyl alcohol between fills; clean again after penicillin, sulfa, or a hazardous drug; use a dedicated tray for hazardous drugs.
Optional sterile garbing only (not core PTCE), dirtiest to cleanest: shoe covers → hair/beard cover → mask → hand hygiene → gown → sterile gloves last.
Vaccine storage: most refrigerated at 2–8°C (36–46°F), do not freeze; monitor with calibrated thermometers and document temps.
NIOSH publishes the List of Hazardous Drugs in Healthcare Settings for safe handling.
USP <797> — standards for compounding sterile preparations.
USP <800> — standards for handling hazardous drugs.
USP <795> — non-sterile compounding chapter (not a dedicated 2026 PTCE procedure skill).

sections.title: Immunization Workflow — VIS, VAERS & Pharmacist Hand-off
items: VIS (Vaccine Information Statement): CDC sheet required by the National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act before each dose of a covered vaccine.
Give the current VIS edition before immunization (not only afterward). Document the VIS publication date and the date it was provided.

Post-immunization care (outline 3.3): for most vaccines, observe seated or lying down for 15 minutes (most syncope is within 15 minutes). Some people are observed for 30 minutes after a COVID-19 vaccine. If the patient feels faint, seat them and notify the pharmacist. Do not send them to drive off untreated.
VAERS reports vaccine adverse events (outline 3.4). MedWatch is the general FDA drug/device program — do not mix the two.
OTC recommendation, therapeutic substitution, DUR/ADE, and allergy/interaction alerts require pharmacist intervention (3.3). Techs gather facts and escalate.

Purple Book (FDA biologics interchangeability) is not a January 2026 PTCE knowledge area — not treated as tested. Orange Book A/AB codes remain the small-molecule TE reference already in Federal notes.

domains.summary: Order Entry and Processing (22.50% as of the January 6, 2026 outline). Sig code interpretation, pharmacy calculations, days supply, conversions, prescription intake, NDC format, and insurance processing. Alligation is not a tested calculation skill on the 2026 outline.

sections.title: Common Sig Codes
items: PO = by mouth; PR = rectally; SL = sublingual; IV/IM/SC = injection routes.
BID = twice daily; TID = 3x daily; QID = 4x daily; QHS = at bedtime; QAM = every morning.
PRN = as needed; ac = before meals; pc = after meals; q6h = every 6 hours.
gtt = drop. OD/OS/OU = right/left/both eyes; AD/AS/AU = right/left/both ears. Error-prone: do not use; write right eye, left eye, both eyes, right ear, left ear, or both ears.
ii tab = 2 tablets; i cap = 1 capsule; qs = quantity sufficient; UD = as directed.
bid — bis in die (twice daily).

sections.title: Key Conversions
items: 1 tsp = 5 mL; 1 tbsp = 15 mL; 1 fl oz = 30 mL; 1 cup = 240 mL.
1 grain (gr) ≈ 65 mg; 1 oz = 28.4 g; 1 g = 1,000 mg; 1 mg = 1,000 mcg.
1 gallon = 3,785 mL; 1 pint = 473 mL; 1 quart = 946 mL.
Temperature: °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9; body 37°C = 98.6°F; fridge 2–8°C = 36–46°F.

sections.title: Core Calculations
items: Days supply = total quantity ÷ amount used per day.
Percent w/v = g per 100 mL (solutions). Percent w/w = g per 100 g (creams, ointments).
Dilution: C1V1 = C2V2.
IV flow rate (mL/hr) = total volume ÷ total time (hr).
Drops/min = (volume × drop factor) ÷ time in minutes.
Alligation (mixing two strengths to an intermediate): removed from the January 2026 PTCE calculation list — not a tested skill.
Powder volume = final volume − diluent added.
Dose by weight = mg/kg × weight (kg).
Dilution: C1V1 = C2V2 (use the same concentration units on both sides).
Reconstitution: total mg in vial ÷ final reconstituted mL = final mg/mL; the final volume may exceed the diluent volume.
IV admixture units/hour: total units ÷ total mL × infusion rate in mL/hr.
BSA (Mosteller): √(height[cm] × weight[kg] / 3600).
Dose by weight: convert lb to kg (÷2.2), then multiply mg/kg by kg.
1:1000 concentration = 1 g per 1000 mL = 1 mg/mL.
D10W = 10 g dextrose per 100 mL.

sections.title: Prescription Intake
items: Verify patient identifiers: full name and date of birth.
Confirm drug, strength, dosage form, quantity, directions, prescriber, and DEA (if controlled).
Check insurance/DUR and allergies before adjudication.
Technicians enter data; the pharmacist performs the final clinical verification.

sections.title: NDC Format
items: National Drug Code = unique 10- or 11-digit, 3-segment number.
Segment 1 = labeler/manufacturer; Segment 2 = product (strength, dosage form); Segment 3 = package size.
Common formats: 5-4-2, 5-3-2, 4-4-2 (padded to 11 digits with a leading zero in the short segment).

sections.title: Insurance / Third-Party Processing
items: BIN routes the claim; PCN sub-routing; Group ID and Member ID identify plan/patient.
DAW codes: 0 = no product selection indicated, 1 = substitution not allowed by prescriber, 2 = substitution allowed, patient requested the brand.
COB = coordination of benefits (primary vs secondary).
Reject codes: 70 = not covered, 75 = prior auth required, 76 = plan limits/refill too soon, 25 = invalid prescriber ID.

sections.title: Auxiliary Labels
items: Take with food: NSAIDs, metformin, iron. Empty stomach: levothyroxine, bisphosphonates.
Avoid alcohol: metronidazole, CNS depressants. Avoid sun: doxycycline, fluoroquinolones, sulfonamides.
May cause drowsiness: opioids, benzos, antihistamines. Shake well: suspensions.
Do not crush/chew: ER/XL/XR/SR, enteric-coated. Do not freeze insulin. Amoxicillin suspension: refrigeration is preferable, not required.

sections.title: Essential Calculations Reference
items: Concentration: ratio 1:1000 = 1 g/1000 mL = 1 mg/mL. Percent w/v = g per 100 mL (0.9% = 0.9 g/100 mL).
Percent to decimal: divide by 100 (0.75% = 0.0075). Percent w/w: mg per g = %×10 (1% cream = 10 mg/g; 0.25% cream = 2.5 mg/g).
Weight-based dose: mg/kg/day × weight in kg. Convert lb→kg by dividing by 2.2.
Alligation (removed from the January 2026 outline): parts of high = target − low; parts of low = high − target. Review only if needed for practice, not as a 2026 tested skill.
IV flow rate: gtt/min = (mL ÷ minutes) × drop factor; mL/hr = total volume ÷ hours.
Days supply: tablets qty ÷ per-day; insulin (mL × 100) ÷ units/day; drops/ sprays multiply mL × 20 (or actuations) ÷ per-day; round down for billing.
Alligation is not on the January 2026 PTCE calculation list; use C1V1 = C2V2 for dilution/concentration instead.
Percentage strength: % w/v = g/100 mL; % v/v = mL/100 mL; % w/w = g/100 g.
Ratio strength: 1:X means 1 g (or mL) per X mL total solution.

sections.title: Reading the Prescription
items: Parts: inscription (drug/strength), subscription (quantity/refills), Signa/sig (patient directions).
"Disp #30" = dispense 30; refills are authorized separately (e.g., "Refills: 2").
DAW codes: 0 = no product selection indicated, 1 = substitution not allowed by prescriber, 2 = substitution allowed, patient requested the brand.
Red flags to clarify with pharmacist: illegible handwriting, unusual dose, missing quantity/sig, or dangerous abbreviation.
Verify patient identity with two identifiers (full name + date of birth) before filling to prevent wrong-patient errors.
Non-controlled: per state law, commonly up to 1 year.

domains.summary: Federal Requirements (18.75% as of the January 6, 2026 outline). DEA schedules and forms, refill, transfer, and C-II partial-fill rules (including CARA 30-day), restricted programs (2.4 REMS/CMEA), pharmaceutical waste (2.1), take-back and CS destruction (Form 41 vs 222), FDA medication recalls (2.5), and DSCSA product tracing (2.6). The DATA 2000 X-waiver was eliminated in December 2022. The Clozapine REMS was removed effective June 13, 2025.

sections.title: DEA Controlled Substance Schedules
items: C-I: no accepted medical use, high abuse (heroin, LSD, and marijuana that is not an FDA-approved product and not under a state medical-marijuana license).

Marijuana split (April 28, 2026): FDA-approved marijuana products and state-licensed medical marijuana are C-III. Other marijuana remains C-I while broader rescheduling is pending. Older “all marijuana is C-I” notes are out of date.
C-II: high abuse, accepted use — NO refills (oxycodone, hydrocodone, morphine, Adderall, fentanyl, methadone). Rx typically valid 30 days (state may vary).
C-III: moderate abuse (Tylenol #3, testosterone, buprenorphine) — up to 5 refills within 6 months of the written date.
C-IV: lower abuse (alprazolam, lorazepam, tramadol, zolpidem, carisoprodol) — up to 5 refills within 6 months of the written date.
C-V: lowest abuse (cough syrups with codeine, pregabalin). Federal law does not set a 5-refill / 6-month cap on Schedule V; follow the stricter state rule.
Tramadol → C-IV (2014); hydrocodone combos → C-II (Oct 6, 2014).

sections.title: DEA Forms
items: Form 222: order/transfer Schedule I & II substances (paper is now single-sheet, not the old triplicate; electronic = CSOS). No alterations; unused executed forms expire in 60 days; keep records 2 years. Destruction/disposal is Form 41, not 222.
Form 106: theft or significant loss. Written notice to the local DEA field office within 1 business day, then electronic Form 106 within 45 calendar days. Paper Form 106 is not accepted.
Form 41: record destruction/disposal of controlled substances.
Form 224: pharmacy application for DEA registration (224a = renewal every 3 years).
CSOS (authorized 2005): electronic ordering of C-I/C-II; requires DEA digital certificate.
DEA Form 222 — order or transfer Schedule I & II (single-sheet paper or CSOS); not for destruction.
DEA Form 106 — theft or significant loss: 1-business-day written notice, then electronic Form 106 within 45 days (no paper).
DEA Form 41 — record destruction/disposal of controlled substances.
DEA Form 224 — pharmacy registration; renewed every 3 years.
Take-back (2.3): unused patient-owned controlled substances go to a DEA-authorized collector, mail-back, or National Take Back event — never back into dispensable stock.

sections.title: Pharmaceutical Waste, OSHA Exposure & Right-to-Know (2.1)
items: P-list = acutely hazardous when the listed chemical is the sole active ingredient. Examples: warfarin above 0.3% (P001); nicotine (P075), except FDA-approved OTC nicotine replacement products.
U-list = toxic, not acute. Examples: cyclophosphamide (U058); lindane (U129). Characteristic hazardous waste (ignitable, corrosive, reactive, toxic) can apply even when a drug is not listed.
2019 EPA rule: do not sewer (flush or drain) hazardous-waste drugs. That nationwide ban is current federal law.

Segregate waste. Common PTCE color map: black = RCRA hazardous pharmaceutical waste; yellow = trace chemotherapy; red = biohazard/sharps; blue or white = non-hazardous pharmaceutical waste. Vendor labels control if they differ.
OSHA needle-stick: never recap by hand; sharps go in a puncture-resistant container; wash, report, and follow post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).
Eyewash and spill kit must be available. Usual tested eyewash flush is 15 minutes, then follow the SDS. Right-to-know: staff can access the SDS for chemicals they handle.

sections.title: Key Federal Laws
items: FDCA (1938): FDA drug safety authority; Durham-Humphrey (1951): Rx vs OTC classification.
Kefauver-Harris (1962): required proof of efficacy (thalidomide disaster).
Controlled Substances Act (1970): created the 5-schedule system; Poison Prevention Packaging Act (1970): child-resistant containers.
OBRA-90 (effective 1993): for each Medicaid beneficiary or caregiver who presents a prescription, an offer to counsel plus prospective DUR. Not limited to new prescriptions.
HIPAA (1996; Privacy 2003, Security 2005): protects patient PHI.

CMEA (2005): 3.6 g of base per day (pseudoephedrine, ephedrine, or phenylpropanolamine); 9 g of base per 30 days, of which not more than 7.5 g of base may be mail-order; photo ID + logbook (name, address, signature), except one package of not more than 60 mg pseudoephedrine.

The DATA 2000 X-waiver for office-based buprenorphine was eliminated in December 2022 (MAT Act). Any DEA-registered practitioner with Schedule III authority may prescribe buprenorphine for OUD; a separate X-waiver is no longer required. DSCSA (2013) is its own 2026 knowledge area (2.6) — see the DSCSA section.
Biennial (every 2 years) controlled substance inventory required.
CSOS — Controlled Substance Ordering System for electronic Schedule II orders.
Controlled-substance prescription records must be maintained for at least 2 years.

C-III–V prescriptions may be transferred one time for a refill, unless the pharmacies share a real-time online database (then until refills are exhausted). An unfilled electronic C-II–V prescription may be transferred once for initial dispensing, pharmacist to pharmacist, at the patient’s request; it stays electronic. Authorized C-III–V refills transfer with it. A paper C-II cannot be transferred. Non-controlled refills transfer as state law allows, with no federal one-time cap.
C-II–IV labels: “Caution: Federal law prohibits the transfer of this drug to any person other than the patient for whom it was prescribed.” Not required on C-V.
C-II receipt: record the date and quantity received on the pharmacy’s copy of Form 222. Returns to a reverse distributor: C-II on Form 222 (or CSOS); C-III–V on an invoice.

C-II partial fills: pharmacy cannot supply → remainder within 72 hours. Patient or prescriber requests a partial (CARA 2016) → remaining portions within 30 days of the written date, except an emergency oral C-II (remaining portions within 72 hours after the prescription is issued). LTCF/terminally ill → 60 days. After the window, leftover quantity needs a new prescription.

sections.title: HIPAA — Tech Specifics
items: PHI = any info identifying the patient (name, DOB, Rx number, diagnosis).
Minimum necessary applies to most uses and disclosures. It does not apply to a disclosure to, or a request by, a health care provider for treatment. Notice of Privacy Practices at first fill.
Permitted disclosures: treatment, payment, operations (TPO) without extra authorization.

Breach notification within 60 days; civil penalties are four inflation-adjusted tiers (2025): minimum $145, $1,461, $14,602, or $73,011 per violation; per-violation maximum $73,011 except $2,190,294 for uncorrected willful neglect; calendar-year cap $2,190,294; plus criminal penalties.

sections.title: PPPA & Pseudoephedrine (CMEA)
items: PPPA (1970): child-resistant packaging for most Rx and certain OTC drugs. Enforced by the CPSC, not the FDA. Sublingual nitroglycerin is exempt (also commonly tested: SL isosorbide, prednisone ≤105 mg per package, certain pediatric antibiotics).
Non-CRC request: a prescriber may request it for a single prescription. Only the patient may make a blanket request for all of their prescriptions. Document the request.
ADA packaging accommodations: easy-off caps, large-print labels, talking labels, and Braille labels.
Medication Guides: give the FDA Medication Guide with each fill of a drug that requires one, including refills.

CMEA: 3.6 g of base per day (pseudoephedrine, ephedrine, or phenylpropanolamine); 9 g of base per 30 days, of which not more than 7.5 g of base may be mail-order; photo ID + logbook (name, address, signature), except one package of not more than 60 mg pseudoephedrine; behind the counter.

sections.title: Restricted Drug Programs (2.4) — REMS & CMEA
items: Knowledge area 2.4: federal restricted programs and related processing — pseudoephedrine (CMEA) and Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies (REMS).

REMS: FDA-required extra safety steps for drugs with serious risks. Common elements: pharmacy/prescriber certification, patient enrollment, a Medication Guide with each fill, and an authorization check before dispense.

Clozapine REMS was removed effective June 13, 2025, so clozapine is not a current pharmacy REMS. Pharmacies do not enroll and do not confirm an ANC through a REMS before dispensing. Severe neutropenia risk, the boxed warning, and a Medication Guide remain. ANC monitoring stays with the prescriber per the labeling.

iPLEDGE (isotretinoin): teratogen. Prescriber, certified pharmacy, and patients enroll — patients who can get pregnant and patients who cannot get pregnant. Maximum 30-day supply, no refills, authorization before each dispense. Patients who can get pregnant have a 7-day pickup window from specimen collection. The old 19-day lockout is not current: a missed window gets a repeat pregnancy test immediately, with no extra wait.

THALOMID/lenalidomide remains a current pregnancy-prevention REMS. TIRF is not a routine current enroll-and-dispense REMS: production of TIRF medicines stopped September 30, 2024, and the REMS accepts no new enrollments. Tech action on a REMS reject: stop and notify the pharmacist.

CMEA (still 2.4): 3.6 g of base per day (pseudoephedrine, ephedrine, or phenylpropanolamine); 9 g of base per 30 days, of which not more than 7.5 g of base may be mail-order; photo ID + logbook; behind the counter or locked.

sections.title: DEA Number Verification
items: Format: 2 letters + 7 digits. First letter = registrant type (B = physician, C = pharmacy, M = mid-level); second letter = registrant's last-name initial.
Check digit math: (1st+3rd+5th digits) + 2×(2nd+4th+6th digits) = sum; the last digit of the sum must equal the 7th (check) digit.
Example: AB1234563 → (1+3+5)=9; (2+4+6)=12 ×2 =24; 9+24=33; last digit 3 = check digit 3. Valid.

sections.title: FDA Medication Recalls (2.5)
items: Outline 2.5 is medication recalls. Recall classes: Class I = reasonable probability of serious adverse health consequences or death; Class II = temporary or medically reversible harm, or a remote probability of serious harm; Class III = adverse health consequences not likely (often labeling/packaging).
Recall depth: wholesale, retail, or consumer (patient) level. A Class I medication recall usually reaches the consumer level, and patients who received the affected lot are notified.
Identify recalled medication by NDC, lot, and expiration, then quarantine affected stock.
The firm initiates a recall. FDA may request one. Pharmacy action is the same: pull, quarantine, document, and follow the recall notice for returns/patient notification.
Market withdrawal is not a recall — the firm removes a product for a minor violation that would not be subject to legal action (e.g., a tamper-evident issue that is not a safety recall).
Orange Book codes: A/AB = therapeutically equivalent (substitutable); B = not equivalent.
NPI: 10-digit provider ID (effective 2007); required on claims; does NOT replace DEA number.
When federal and state rules differ, follow the stricter requirement.
On any recall: match NDC + lot + expiration, quarantine, document, and follow the notice for returns and patient notification. Class I is pulled immediately.
Take-back programs (2.3) are for unwanted patient-owned drugs (especially controls). A recall is a firm/FDA action on specific lots still in the supply chain — do not mix the two workflows.

sections.title: DSCSA — Drug Supply Chain Security Act (2.6)
items: DSCSA (2013, Title II of DQSA) is knowledge area 2.6 on the January 2026 outline: product tracing, handling, and records for recall and investigation of suspect/illegitimate product.
Serialization: each package carries a unique product identifier (usually a 2D data matrix) with NDC, serial number, lot number, and expiration date.

Current exchange is electronic Transaction Information (TI) and a Transaction Statement (TS). Transaction History (TH) was retired in November 2023. Do not memorize a mandatory TI + TH + TS trio as current law.

Authorized trading partners: manufacturers, wholesale distributors, dispensers (pharmacies), and repackagers that are appropriately licensed/registered. Dispensers may accept product only from authorized partners.
Suspect product: reason to believe it may be counterfeit, diverted, stolen, intentionally adulterated, or otherwise unfit. Illegitimate product: credible evidence that it is one of those things.

Suspect product: do not dispense; quarantine; notify the pharmacist; verify the product identifier (NDC, serial, lot, expiration). Once the product is confirmed illegitimate, notify FDA (Form FDA 3911) and immediate trading partners within 24 hours.
Keep DSCSA transaction records for 6 years. FDA used phased implementation milestones for electronic package-level tracing; learn the durable duties above rather than a specific exemption end-date.

sections.title: Counseling & Omnibus Laws
items: OBRA-90: for each Medicaid beneficiary or caregiver who presents a prescription, prospective DUR and a pharmacist offer to counsel. The offer is not limited to new prescriptions. The patient may decline.

HIPAA: protects PHI; provide a Notice of Privacy Practices. Minimum necessary applies to most uses and disclosures. It does not apply to a disclosure to, or a request by, a health care provider for treatment.
FDCA 1938 (safety), Durham-Humphrey 1951 (Rx vs OTC), Kefauver-Harris 1962 (safety + efficacy, GMP).
Controlled Substances Act 1970: created the five DEA schedules; enforced by the DEA.

Poison Prevention Packaging Act 1970: child-resistant containers, enforced by the CPSC. Sublingual nitroglycerin is exempt. A prescriber may request non-CRC for one prescription; only the patient may make a blanket request.
Medication Guides are dispensed with each fill of specified drugs, including refills.

Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act: 3.6 g of base per day (pseudoephedrine, ephedrine, or phenylpropanolamine); 9 g of base per 30 days, of which not more than 7.5 g of base may be mail-order; photo ID + logbook; behind the counter.
